problems.statement: The spring service change cut recovery (layover) time on 21 of 38 routes from 8% to 15% median, so late inbound arrivals cascade into late next-trip departures; this is a major cause of the OTP decline.

Lane reductions from Halvorsen Avenue and Bridgeport Road construction roughly doubled running times in the work zones on routes 9, 14, 22, 31 and 33, causing a second step-down; on these routes it compounds the recovery cut and accounts for the largest share of lateness.
The 40% absenteeism rise is the cause of the OTP decline (the client's explanation).
The +40% absence figure is largely a measurement artifact of the ShiftLine go-live on 2026-03-30, which began recording partial-day absences as occurrences; full-day absences rose only 1.1%.
OTP measurement or AVL error explains the decline.
Passenger load or dwell time increases explain the decline.
Route-agnostic extraboard coverage by unfamiliar spare operators, and garage differences, explain the decline.

Tight layovers cause operators to leave early (partial-day absences), a feedback loop that pushes real absences up in future; supported only by an association confounded by seniority, age and route length, with no pre-April data.
The size of the recovery-cut effect separate from the construction effect on Group A is not cleanly separable.

causalClaims.from: Recovery time cut on 21 routes (spring service change)
causalClaims.to: Late first-timepoint departures and lower OTP on Group B

causalClaims.from: Construction lane reductions on Halvorsen and Bridgeport corridors
causalClaims.to: Longer running times and further OTP drop on Group A routes

causalClaims.from: Absence count rise and OTP drop timing coincidence in April

actions.action: Do not roll out the tougher attendance program (discipline at 3 occurrences in 90 days) counting ShiftLine partial-day occurrences, and do not take it to the board as planned.
actions.rationale: Absenteeism did not drive OTP, the increase is a recording artifact, and the policy would punish illness or early leaves, likely worsening labor relations without fixing OTP.

actions.action: Restore recovery time on the 21 routes, prioritizing the five corridor routes and the longest routes, for example by funding extra buses or trimming Route 51 resources.
actions.rationale: This is the largest controllable cause affecting 60% of trips, and Group B shows it with no construction confound.

actions.action: Re-time the five construction-corridor routes with running times that reflect the work-zone delay (13 and 9.5 min segments), and coordinate with Public Works on detours, signal priority or transit lanes.
actions.rationale: Scheduled running times were never updated for the work zones, which last until August 2027, so lateness is built into the schedule.

actions.action: Correct the board narrative: restate absence metrics separating full-day from partial-day, and respond to the May schedule grievance with the union.
actions.rationale: Fixes the misread metric, restores credibility, and addresses an unanswered grievance.

actions.action: Run a communications plan to the union framed around a punitive attendance policy.
actions.rationale: It would promote a misdiagnosis and deepen distrust.

actions.action: Review partial-day absences, such as early leaves, for operator health and fatigue after layover cuts, and design an attendance policy that only counts full-day absences.
actions.rationale: The early-leave pattern is a possible welfare and retention concern, but its cause is unconfirmed.

actions.action: Hire more extraboard operators or change extraboard route assignments.
actions.rationale: Dispatch log shows missed trips and late pull-outs are unchanged, so coverage is not the constraint.

nextEvidence: Early-leave rates by route length, seniority and recovery time (regression or within-route comparison) to test whether tight layovers drive partial-day absences
Pilot results from restoring recovery time on a subset of Group B routes (OTP before and after) to size the effect
Group A vs Group B decomposition of construction versus recovery contributions, including post-April-20 weekly trends and hold-at-terminal data
output.summary: The absenteeism story does not hold. The +40% is a measurement artifact: ShiftLine began recording partial-day absences in late March, and full-day absences rose only 1.1%. Dispatch data show no change in missed trips or late pull-outs. The OTP decline comes from two compounding causes. First, the April 5 recovery-time cut on 21 routes, which hurt Group B with no construction (81.6 to 71.5%). Second, the April 20 construction on five of those routes, which added a larger drop (83.5 to 52.5%). Routes with neither change held at 82%. Do not roll out the attendance policy. Restore layovers and re-time the construction routes. Whether tight layovers drive early leaves remains uncertain.
